newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Price leap piles pressure on German gas oil buyers.
newsitem.headline: Price leap piles pressure on German gas oil buyers.

text.p: German gas oil users who have bought only essential requirements since spring and patiently waited for price falls, faced a rude shock this week as hostilities in Iraq send prices soaring.
A number of smaller dealers are clamouring to cover unhedged shorts and refiners are wrestling to keep sales at a minimum lest prices rise even higher.
"We have told our salespeople to keep an eye on the quantities and just sell the scheduled amount," said a trader at one German refiner.
"We have huge volumes of middle distillate stocks, but we have cut the volumes per customer and we are selling very carefully," said another.
A similar fear of further hostilities and thus further price rises have left dealers in Germany desperate to stock up to brace themselves for a surge of consumer demand.
"If they could, (the dealers) would have bought much more than they have been given," said a German trader.
"The dealers are preparing for a rush. There's quite a bit of money to be made," said another.

German household heating oil stocks rose modestly in summer from 51 percent of capacity at the end of June to 55 percent at the end of July. This was still 10 percent lower than at the same time last year.
German consumers of heating oil who have patiently awaited price falls since spring now feel the first hint of cold weather with heating oil prices at their highest level since November 1991.
Benchmark September gas oil futures prices have risen $17 a tonne, or 8.6 percent from Friday's close to $213.00 a tonne at midsession Tuesday.
The rise of the dollar, partly the result of Gulf tensions, has also exacerbated the situation for the German consumer.
Traders in the key Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp market face lesser problems, but the tranquillity of the cash market belies the animated nature of discussions.

Many buyers will have hedged their immediate requirements against futures, but most have delayed additional purchases as the IPE futures. The abstinence of buyers in the ARA market is expected to lead to higher gas oil premiums for barges.
"A lot of people are just shell-shocked and are waiting for some correction, but there are many worried that it won't happen," said one trader.
The timing for some could not be worse.
Refinery maintenance is due to start, the traditional build-up of heating oil stocks is underway and this year there is a new requirement for low sulphur diesel inventories.
"There are a lot of people short overall. That's where you see the panic," said one ARA trader.
"Even if they don't lose money, it will be a nightmare of calculations," another said.
